title: The Beginning of the Gospel
summary: Mark opens with John the Baptist preaching repentance in the wilderness and announcing a mightier one to come. Jesus is baptized, hears the Father's voice, and is driven by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tested. Then he announces the kingdom of God in Galilee, calls four fishermen, drives out an unclean spirit in the Capernaum synagogue, heals Simon's mother-in-law and many others, withdraws to pray, and cleanses a leper who then spreads the news everywhere.
story: Mark begins abruptly, with no birth story and no genealogy. His first line names his subject, the good news of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, and his second reaches back to Israel's prophets, who promised that God would send a messenger to prepare his way and would come himself to rescue his people. John is that messenger. From there the chapter moves at a run: within forty-five verses Jesus is baptized, tested, preaching, calling disciples, and exercising authority over evil spirits and disease. By the end his fame has spread so widely that he can no longer enter a town openly. The chapter sets out the book's main threads: who Jesus is, the arrival of God's kingdom, his authority, and the call to follow.
historical:
The events are set in the late 20s AD, during the reign of the emperor Tiberius. Galilee in the north was ruled by Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, while Judea and Jerusalem were under the Roman governor Pontius Pilate. John the Baptist is known outside the New Testament: the Jewish historian Josephus describes him as a good man who called Jews to righteousness and baptism, and says Antipas imprisoned and executed him at the fortress of Machaerus east of the Dead Sea, fearing his influence with the crowds. Mark's reference to John's arrest in verse 14 anticipates that story, told in chapter 6.

Capernaum was a fishing town on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee, a lake about thirteen miles long, near a border and a road, which made it a good base for a traveling teacher. Excavations there have uncovered a large limestone synagogue from several centuries after Jesus, built over an earlier foundation that some archaeologists think belongs to the synagogue of his day, and a house under an ancient church that was venerated early on as Peter's home. Those identifications are debated, but they show that the Capernaum of the Gospels was a real and modest place.
cultural:
John's clothing of camel's hair and a leather belt recalls the prophet Elijah (2 Kings 1:8), and many Jews expected Elijah to return before the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5). His diet of locusts and wild honey was the food of the wilderness, and locusts were among the insects the law permitted (Leviticus 11:22). Baptism, from a Greek word meaning to dip or immerse, echoed Jewish ritual washings for purity, but John's was a once-for-all washing tied to repentance, a turning of the whole life back to God. Untying a master's sandals was the lowliest work of a slave, which is why John says he is not worthy to do it.

The synagogue was the local meeting place for prayer, reading of the Scriptures, and teaching, and a visiting teacher could be invited to speak. The scribes taught by citing earlier authorities; Jesus taught on his own authority. Leprosy in the Bible covers a range of skin diseases described in Leviticus 13 and 14, not only what is now called Hansen's disease. Those with it were ritually unclean and lived apart, and touching one made a person unclean, so Jesus' touch in verse 41 would have startled onlookers. A healed person had to be examined by a priest and offer sacrifices before returning to community life.
literary: Mark's opening is compressed and quick. The Greek word usually translated “immediately” or “at once” appears eleven times in this chapter alone and drives the action forward. The chapter falls into a prologue (verses 1 to 13), which tells the reader who Jesus is before any character in the story knows, and the start of the Galilean ministry. Verses 21 to 39 describe what is often called a day in Capernaum, a Sabbath from the synagogue to the evening crowds, followed by prayer before dawn. Watch the commands to silence (verses 25, 34, 44), a feature of Mark that reappears through the first half of the book. The opening quotation combines words from Malachi 3:1 (with Exodus 23:20) and Isaiah 40:3 under the name of Isaiah, the more prominent prophet, a practice found elsewhere in ancient Jewish writing.

outline.t: John the Baptist prepares the way
Healings at Simon's house and at the door

doctrines.note: Jesus' first words in Mark announce that the time is fulfilled and the kingdom of God has come near. The healings and exorcisms that follow show what God's reign looks like as it breaks into a world held by illness and evil.

At the baptism the Son comes up from the water, the Spirit descends on him, and the Father speaks from heaven. Mark does not develop a doctrine, but the scene became one of the church's key texts for confessing one God in three persons.

Both John and Jesus call for repentance, a turning of mind and life toward God, joined to belief in the good news. The first disciples show what it looks like: they leave nets, boats, and even a father to follow Jesus.

words.note: Euthys, immediately or at once, Mark's signature word, used more than forty times across the Gospel and eleven times in this chapter. It sometimes means simply next or then, but its sheer frequency gives Mark's story its breathless pace and its sense that with Jesus, God's action has arrived.

Euangelion, gospel or good news. In the Roman world the word was used for announcements of a victory or of the birth or accession of an emperor. Isaiah 52:7 speaks of messengers bringing good news that God reigns. Mark uses it for the announcement that God's reign has arrived in Jesus.

Exousia, authority, the right and power to act. The crowd in the synagogue is amazed that Jesus teaches with authority and that even unclean spirits obey him. His authority, over spirits, disease, sin, and the Sabbath, is a major theme of Mark's opening chapters.

Splanchnizomai, to be moved with compassion, from a word for the inner organs, felt as the seat of emotion. It describes Jesus' response to the leper. A few ancient manuscripts read that Jesus was moved with anger instead; if that reading is original, the anger is probably at the disease or the man's situation, not at the man.

christ: Mark's first verse tells the reader who Jesus is: the Christ, meaning the anointed king Israel awaited, and the Son of God. The Father confirms it at the baptism, echoing Psalm 2:7 (the royal son) and Isaiah 42:1 (the servant in whom God delights). Isaiah 40's promise of a way prepared for the Lord is applied to Jesus, so that his coming is presented as the coming of Israel's God. He is tested in the wilderness as Israel was, and faithful where Israel failed. He calls people to follow him personally, touches the untouchable, and prays in the dark before dawn. Some early manuscripts lack the words Son of God in verse 1, but the title stands at the Gospel's climax, on the centurion's lips at the cross (15:39).

hard.q: Why does Jesus keep telling demons and the people he heals to be silent about him?
hard.a: The commands to silence puzzle readers, especially since the healed leper disobeys and the news spreads anyway. In 1901 the German scholar William Wrede argued that this messianic secret was a literary device created by the early church to explain why Jesus was not recognized as Messiah during his lifetime. Most scholars now think the pattern has deeper roots in Jesus' own ministry. Several explanations fit the text. Jesus refused the testimony of demons, whose confession was not faith and whose timing he would not accept. He avoided being taken for a political messiah in an atmosphere where messianic claims could spark revolt and bring Roman reprisal. Crowds seeking miracles could hinder his preaching, as verse 45 shows. And, most importantly for Mark, Jesus' identity could not be rightly understood until the cross and resurrection; after the transfiguration he tells the disciples to tell no one until the Son of Man has risen (9:9). The silence is lifted when the meaning of his messiahship is clear.

questions: The first disciples left their nets at once. What would following Jesus require you to leave, or to hold more loosely?
Jesus rose before dawn to pray even when everyone was looking for him. What does that suggest about the relationship between prayer and a busy life?
Jesus touched a man everyone else kept at a distance. Who are the people your community keeps at arm's length, and what would it mean to reach out a hand?
